OSCAR SENTENCE

By: Este de Klerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
After tAfter the SCA overturned Oscar Pistorius's conviction to murder, his defence team and the state led evidence in mitigation and aggravation of sentence.Now his murder sentence awaits.

Summary:
After the Supreme Court of Appeal overturned Oscar Pistorius's initial culpable homicide conviction to one of murder in December 2015, the state and his defence team called witnesses to testify in aggravation and mitigation of his sentence on murder.
The same Judge in which Oscar stood trial for 49 court days spanning eight months in 2014 - Judge Masipa - who initially found him guilty of culpable homicide and sentenced him to five years in prison according to section 276 (1)(i) of the Criminal Procedures Act, meaning he had to serve one sixth of his sentence, now has to sentence him for murder.

Further information:
The Defence's main witness was Professor Jonathan Scholtz who testified that Oscar Pistorius was a "broken and ill man who should be hospitilised". Professor Scholtz testified that further imprisonment would be detrimental to Oscar.
Professor Scholtz was one of a team of psychologists who evaluated Oscar when he was sent to Weskoppies Psychiatric Hospital for observation during his trial in 2014. In the month before asentencing proceedings, the defence team asked Professor Scholtz to evaluate Oscar again.
He found that his psychological conditional deteriorated severely - that he is depressed and anxious - and to such a degree that he was unable to testify during the sentencing proceedings.

Throughout the sentencing proceedings, Oscar looked dazed and forlorn, despite his overwhelming family support.

In a surprise move during adv Barry Roux's closing arguments, he asked Oscar to remove his prosthesis and to stand in front of Judge Masipa on his stumps. Adv Roux said that that is the man who should be judged by Judge Masipa - one who was vulnerable, one with a disability, one who suffered from an anxiety disorder.

Adv Roux also said that the public at large still has the perception that Oscar intentionally killed Reeva. That despite the Supreme Court of Appeal's finding that Oscar was guilty of murder Dolus Eventualis, and NOT of murder dolus directus - didn't matter in the bigger picture of the public's perception - his reputation will never recover because he will always be branded as a murderer.

The State's main witness was Reeva Steenkamp's father, Barry Steenkamp, who himself seemed to be a broken man. Trembling in the witness stand, he told the court what it has done to him and his family since Reeva's died. Barry Steenkamp testified he thought of her every moment of every day, that he had almost become a recluse and that he couldn't stop thinking of the pain and agony she must have endured during the last moments of her life.
He testified how he tried to hurt himself to try and feel the same pain she must have felt.
Barry Steenkamp said it had been very difficult for him to forgive and that Oscar should pay for what he did.
He also asked the Judge that pictures of what Reeva looked like after she had been shot, should be released for the public to see what Oscar did to her and to maybe deter further criminals from doing the same.
Adv Gerrie Nel brought an official application to relase six of the photograghs of Reeva's corpse and Judge Masipa granted the order. The released pictures were mainly published by international newspapers and magazines, except for The New Age who splashed one of the pictures on its front page and You Magazine who published it online.

Judge Masipa postpone court proceedings for three weeks until Wednesday, the 6th of July to sentence Oscar Pistorius for murder.
According to the Criminal Procedures Act the minimum sentence for murder is 15 years. A Judge can use discretion to give a lesser sentence if substantial and compelling circumstances exist. The year that Oscar had already served in jail will most likely be taken into consideration, as well as the four months he served under correctional supervision after he was released from prison in October last year and before the SCA overturned his conviction to murder. He is disabled and the evidence of Professor Scholtz of how Oscar's psychological condition deteriorated over the past two years, will also most likely be taken into consideration when he is sentenced.

Aggravating to his consideration of sentence would be the SCA's findings that Oscar had not offered an explanation of why he fired the four shots and that he must have foreseen and therefore did foresee that he would kill the person behind the door - he was therefore found guilty on murder dolus eventualis.
Chief State prosecutor Gerrie Nel also argued that the fact that Oscar still showed no remorse, the fact that he chose to grant a television interview instead of taking the stand in his sentencing proceedings, should also serve as aggravating circumstances.

Legal experts are divided as to what his sentence will be.

Press Release:


Sentencing Oscar
This week, over three years since Reeva Steenkamp was shot and killed by Paralympian Oscar Pistorius, the world witnessed the latest chapter of a protracted trial that has sustained global attention. Pretoria High Court Judge Thokozile Masipa said the mitigating factors outweighed the aggravating factors and therefore the prescribed 15-year minimum sentence for murder would be unjust. Carte Blanche brings key insight and analysis to the shamed athlete’s new sentence - six years’ imprisonment.


Script:


OSCAR SENTENCE

PRODUCER: ESTÉ DE KLERK

PRESENTER: JOHN WEBB

BROADCAST DATE: 10 JULY 2016

JUDGE MASIPA: The determination of an appropriate sentence that satisfies every relevant interest is never easy. It is made even more difficult by the fact that nothing that this court will do or say today shall bring back the life of the deceased. The life of the accused shall also never be the same. He is a fallen hero, who has lost his career and is ruined financially. The worst is that having taken the life of a fellow human being in the manner that he did, he cannot be at peace.

Reeva Steenkamp is gone forever.
Oscar Pistorius ’s life has changed irrevocably.
As the Supreme Court of Appeal said when it overturned his original conviction of culpable homicide to murder dolus eventualis: “It’s a tragedy of Shakespearean proportions”.

Judge Thokozile Masipa, who on Wednesday this week sentenced Oscar for a second time, said it came as no surprise to her that Oscar was described as a “broken man” during sentencing arguments last month.
In comparison to last month’s visibly distraught Oscar, he was emotionless on Wednesday.
JUDGE MASIPA: The sentence that I impose on the accused for the murder dolus eventualis of the deceased that is Reeva Steenkamp is six years imprisonment.

Clinical Psychologist, “Dr D” says Oscar would have been well-prepared for his sentence.

DR. D: He probably hasn’t been able to think of much else. For him, it was the best outcome he could have wished for.

Criminal defence attorney, Cliffie Alexander says he wasn’t surprised by Judge Masipa’s six year sentence. Technically - according to the Criminal Procedure Act – Oscar has to serve three years – 50 percent – of his prison term.

CLIFFIE: What Oscar could do is within 6-8 months should he behave himself he could approach the relevant parties in correctional services to be considered for parole.

The prescribed minimum sentence for murder is 15 years unless there are substantial and compelling circumstances to justify a lesser sentence. It doesn’t define those circumstances, but leaves it to the discretion of the judge, who must also consider the aggravating and mitigating factors.

As aggravating factors, Judge Masipa echoed the findings of the Appeal Court:

JUDGE MASIPA: The accused used a lethal weapon and fired not one, but four shots into the toilet door, knowing full-well that there was someone behind the door. The toilet was a small cubicle and there was no room for escape for the person behind the door. The accused had been trained in the use of and in the handling of firearms. He used a firearm without taking the precaution of firing a warning shot.

As mitigating factors she cited Oscar’s belief that there was an intruder in his house, his vulnerability on his stumps, his attempt to save Reeva’s life, his remorse and the public’s perception of what happened.

JUDGE MASIPA: It is my view that it must be one of the most difficult things for any accused to have to face the victims of his crime and to apologise. It is highly improbable therefore that the accused would persist in his request to meet the parents of the deceased and ask for forgiveness if he was not genuinly remorseful.

During his testimony in aggravation of sentence, a trembling Barry Steenkamp described how his daughter’s death has devastated the family and that despite Oscar’s offers to meet with them, they weren’t yet ready.

JOHN LINK: Judge Masipa considered public perception a mitigating factor in this trial, in other words she accepted the view that some in society continued to willfully misrepresent the facts presented in the trial and for that reason continued to believe, wrongly so, that Oscar marched down the passage with evil intent.

JUDGE MASIPA: Both the accused and the deceased were well-known. It is therefore not surprising that there would be an unprecedented level of interest in the proceedings and in the outcome. Society has a right to certain expectations, and to demand justice. However, such expectations must be ligitimate expectations before the court can take heed of them.

CLIFFIE: My opinion in eyes of judge, and rightly so, counts for naught.

In an unexpected move during the defence’s closing arguments last month, Barry Roux asked Oscar to remove his prosthetic legs and stand on his stumps.

Judge Masipa said she was convinced by the defence’s case that there are two Oscars: the professional athlete on his prosthetic legs and the vulnerable anxious man on his stumps.

DR. D: His whole life he has been trying not to have the two Oscars. He worked hard at maintaining the one Oscar and of then of course he couldn't’.

Dr D says Oscar’s capacity to overcome his disability and become a Paralympic medallist, will play to his advantage in prison.

DR. D: I believe with the anxiety he has at the moment, especially the Post traumatic stress and the degree of depression that has been referred to - that component hasn’t gone out. And I think that he will bring it to bear to cope with this. Hopefully this has resulted in his ability to be more authentic than he has ever been before his life.

The State argued for a long-term imprisonment, but Judge Masipa said it would do no justice.

JOHN: So in this particular case, those compelling reasons were in fact significant to reduce the minimum by so much?

CLIFFIE: Oscar’s version remains uncontested as to why he shot into that cubicle. That remains uncontested. Oscar is the only person who knows what really happened there. His version, as good or bad as he was a witness he was in court, that is the version we had before us and the Judge believed it. It was taken to be substantial and compelling.

And perhaps the Judge anticipated some outrage at her six-year sentence.

JUDGE MASIPA: It was the court’s duty to impose an appropriate and fair sentence – fearlessly, even if the sentence did not satisfy the public.

CLIFFIE: I personally believe that the State will in all probability appeal this. I think a precedent, to a large extent, has been set. People are actually quite angry. They’re asking: “How could this have happen. How did this happen?”

The Judge said Oscar’s rehabilitation was possible, but would depend on his attitude.

JUDGE MASIPA: Punishment is not what you choose to do, it is something that is imposed on you. By it’s very nature punishment is unpleasant, it is uncomfortable, it is painful and it is inconvenient. It is certainly not what you love to do.

JOHN LINK: In the end Judge Masipa found that the mitigating outweighed the aggravating factors, in other words there were compelling reasons to deviate from the 15-year minimum sentence. The question now is whether the 6-year she’s arrived at will signal the end of this tragic saga.

Oscar’s team says it won’t be appealing Oscar’s sentence.
But the State has another week and a half to decide if it wants to apply for leave to appeal in order to secure a longer jail sentence for the former Paralympian.





PROMO’S

PROMO 1:15”

CLIFFIE: A precedent to a large extent has been set. People are actually quite angry.

(11”) Oscar Pistorius is back in prison. Is this the end to the tragic saga or will the State apply for leave to appeal the 6-year murder sentenced Judge Masipa imposed on him?

PROMO 2:15”

(15”) Judge Masipa found that the mitigating outweighed the aggravating factors, in other words there were compelling reasons to deviate from the 15-year minimum sentence. The question now is whether the six years she’s arrived at will signal the end of this tragic saga?

Barry Steenkamp said it had been very difficult for him to forgive and that Oscar should pay for what he did. He also asked the Judge that pictures of what Reeva looked like after she had been shot, should be released for the public to see what Oscar did to her and to maybe deter further criminals from doing the same. Adv Gerrie Nel brought an official application to relase six of the photograghs of Reeva's corpse and Judge Masipa granted the order. The released pictures were mainly published by international newspapers and magazines, except for The New Age who splashed one of the pictures on its front page and You Magazine who published it online. Judge Masipa postpone court proceedings for three weeks until Wednesday, the 6th of July to sentence Oscar Pistorius for murder. According to the Criminal Procedures Act the minimum sentence for murder is 15 years. A Judge can use discretion to give a lesser sentence if substantial and compelling circumstances exist. The year that Oscar had already served in jail will most likely be taken into consideration, as well as the four months he served under correctional supervision after he was released from prison in October last year and before the SCA overturned his conviction to murder. He is disabled and the evidence of Professor Scholtz of how Oscar's psychological condition deteriorated over the past two years, will also most likely be taken into consideration when he is sentenced. Aggravating to his consideration of sentence would be the SCA's findings that Oscar had not offered an explanation of why he fired the four shots and that he must have foreseen and therefore did foresee that he would kill the person behind the door - he was therefore found guilty on murder dolus eventualis. Chief State prosecutor Gerrie Nel also argued that the fact that Oscar still showed no remorse, the fact that he chose to grant a television interview instead of taking the stand in his sentencing proceedings, should also serve as aggravating circumstances. Legal experts are divided as to what his sentence will be.
